en: To praise enthusiastically and publicly; public praise
hook: AC-CLAIM: everyone CLAIMS it's great — loudly.
story: Acclaim. A young Bangladeshi director made her first feature film on a tiny budget, shooting in her grandmother's village with local actors. She sent it to an international festival without much hope. At the premiere, the audience stood and applauded for ten minutes. Critics from Paris to Tokyo praised it. The film received worldwide acclaim: enthusiastic public praise. As a verb, to acclaim is to praise publicly. Critical acclaim means strong praise from experts.

gre.s: Although her early novels were ignored, her final book won universal ____, earning every major literary prize that year.
gre.clue: earning every major literary prize that year

example: The young cricketer from Sylhet was acclaimed across the country after scoring a century in his very first test match.

en: Very skilled or proficient at something
hook: ADEPT: an ADEPT is an ADEPT-ed expert.
story: Adept. Nobody in Kamal's family could fix anything electrical, except his twelve-year-old niece. She repaired the broken ceiling fan, replaced a frayed charger cable, and even brought the old radio back to life using online videos and a tiny screwdriver. Everyone agreed she was adept at repairs: very skilled and proficient. Adept is usually followed by at or in. Do not mix it up with inept, which sounds similar but means clumsy and unskilled. Synonyms: skilled, expert, proficient.

gre.s: Although new to the job, she proved remarkably ____ at calming angry customers, defusing complaints that had defeated her far more experienced colleagues.
gre.clue: defusing complaints that had defeated her far more experienced colleagues

example: My grandmother is so adept at bargaining that vendors at Kawran Bazar lower their prices the moment they see her coming.

en: To learn for sure, usually by checking carefully
hook: AS-CERTAIN: make CERTAIN.
story: Ascertain. A rumour spread through the hostel that the bus to Sylhet would leave at five instead of seven. Some students rushed to the station at dawn. Nadia did not trust rumours. She called the bus company twice, then checked their website, to ascertain the real departure time. It was seven. To ascertain is to find something out for certain. Investigators work to ascertain the cause of an accident. Think: make certain.

gre.s: Before publishing the story, the editor insisted that reporters ____ the facts from at least two independent sources.
gre.clue: from at least two independent sources

example: Before signing the lease, Rumana phoned the previous tenants to ascertain whether the flat really stayed dry during the monsoon.

en: Highly ornate and extravagant in style; excessively complicated
hook: BAROQUE: so ornate it might BREAK under all the decoration.
story: Baroque. The wedding stage at the Gulshan convention hall was unbelievable: golden pillars carved with peacocks, crystal chandeliers, ten thousand roses, mirrors on every surface, and a fountain spraying coloured water. Not one inch was left plain. Guests did not know where to look first. It was baroque: highly ornate, extravagant, even excessively complicated. Baroque originally named a richly decorated European art style. A baroque plot has far too many twists.

gre.s: Readers accustomed to the author's spare early style were startled by the ____ prose of her later novels, with their elaborate, ornamented sentences.
gre.clue: with their elaborate, ornamented sentences

example: The tax form was so baroque, with its endless sub-clauses and cross-references, that even the accountant needed a whole afternoon to finish it.

en: Well-meaning and kind; charitable
hook: BENE-VOLENT: wishing (vol) good (bene).
story: Benevolent. Every winter, Ishita's grandfather, a retired schoolteacher in Rangpur, spends part of his pension on blankets. He walks from house to house in the poorest part of town, handing them out quietly, without taking photographs or telling anyone. He is benevolent: well-meaning, kind, and charitable. Bene means good and vol means wish, as in volunteer: a benevolent person wishes others well. Its opposite is malevolent, wishing harm. Synonyms: kind, generous, philanthropic.

gre.s: Far from being the ____ patron he appeared to be in public, the landlord privately evicted any tenant who fell even a single week behind on rent.
gre.clue: privately evicted any tenant who fell even a single week behind on rent

example: The mill owner was remembered as a benevolent employer who quietly paid school fees for every worker's children.

en: To support or strengthen
hook: BOLSTER: a BOLSTER is a long pillow that props you up.
story: Bolster. Ishita's research proposal made a bold claim: that mangrove forests reduce cyclone deaths by half. Her supervisor frowned. "Bold claims need strong support." So Ishita added data from four countries, interviews with two experts, and twenty maps. At the final presentation, nobody could find a weak point. She had bolstered her argument: supported and strengthened it. A bolster is a long, firm pillow that props you up. A good mock score bolsters your confidence.

gre.s: The prosecutor hoped the new forensic evidence would ____ a case that had, until then, rested almost entirely on a single witness.
gre.clue: rested almost entirely on a single witness

example: A run of easy wins early in the tournament bolstered the young team's confidence before they faced the defending champions.

en: Settling a question completely, leaving no room for doubt
hook: CONCLUSIVE: brings the argument to a CONCLUSION.
story: Conclusive. For weeks, Lamia's hostel argued about who was stealing milk from the shared fridge. Everyone had a theory, but nobody had proof. Then the warden checked the corridor camera. The footage showed the night guard quietly drinking it at two in the morning. That was conclusive evidence: proof beyond doubt. Conclusive is related to conclude: it brings an argument to an end. Do not confuse it with conducive, which means helpful. Synonyms: decisive, definitive, irrefutable.

gre.s: Although the early studies were suggestive, they were far from ____, and regulators insisted on a much larger trial before declaring the drug effective.
gre.clue: insisted on a much larger trial before declaring the drug effective

example: DNA testing finally gave conclusive proof that the bones belonged to the explorer who vanished in the Arctic in 1845.

en: Causing or likely to cause argument; quarrelsome
hook: CONTENTIOUS: creates CONTENTION (conflict).
story: Contentious. At Eid dinner, someone mentioned the upcoming election. Within thirty seconds, uncles were shouting, aunties were taking sides, and a cousin had stormed off to the balcony. Grandmother banged her spoon on the table: "No politics at dinner!" Politics in that family is a contentious topic: likely to cause argument. A contentious person loves to argue. Contention means dispute. GRE passages often discuss contentious scientific debates.

gre.s: The proposal to build the dam proved highly ____, provoking furious debates in parliament and protests across the region.
gre.clue: provoking furious debates in parliament and protests

example: A plan to cut down the old banyan tree in the village square and pave a parking lot turned contentious within days.

en: The feeling that something is unworthy of respect; to scorn
hook: DIS-DAIN: you won't DEIGN to look at it.
story: Disdain. At a fancy restaurant in Banani, a wealthy man glanced at the menu, then at the waiter, and said, 'I do not eat this cheap food.' He pushed the plate away with two fingers as if it were dirty. His face showed disdain: the feeling that something is unworthy of respect. As a verb, to disdain is to scorn, so a proud person may disdain to answer a rude question. Dis means not, and the root means worthy. Synonyms: contempt, scorn.

gre.s: The aristocrat made no effort to hide his ____ for the newly rich merchants, refusing their invitations and mocking their manners at every opportunity.
gre.clue: mocking their manners at every opportunity

example: The veteran chef spoke of instant noodles with open disdain, though his students often caught him eating them late at night.

en: To break up and move off in many directions
hook: DIS-PERSE: like a SPRAY spreading out.
story: Disperse. Thousands of people gathered at Shahbag for an evening rally. When a sudden thunderstorm broke, they ran in every direction: under shop awnings, into rickshaws, down side streets. Within ten minutes the square was empty. The crowd had dispersed: scattered over a wide area. Wind disperses seeds, and police may disperse a crowd. Di means apart, and the root means to scatter. Opposite: gather, assemble. Synonyms: scatter, dissipate.

gre.s: Once the morning fog began to ____, the hikers could see the trail clearly again, though only an hour earlier the valley had been completely hidden.
gre.clue: the hikers could see the trail clearly again

example: Wind and ocean currents dispersed the oil slick along hundreds of kilometres of coastline within a single week.

en: So firmly fixed that it is very hard to remove
hook: EN-TRENCHED: dug deep into a TRENCH, impossible to move.
story: Entrenched. The government banned dowry decades ago. Yet in some villages, families still quietly exchange cash, furniture, and motorbikes at weddings. Change is slow because the custom is entrenched: firmly established and very difficult to change. Picture soldiers dug deep into a trench, impossible to move. Entrenched beliefs, entrenched interests, entrenched corruption. Reformers must dig them out patiently, one family at a time.

gre.s: Reformers found it difficult to challenge the ____ bureaucracy, whose habits and privileges had been established over generations.
gre.clue: established over generations

example: The rivalry between the two neighbouring football clubs is so entrenched that grandfathers still argue about a match played in 1975.

en: Not regular or predictable; inconsistent
hook: ERRATIC: full of ERRORS, all over the place.
story: Erratic. Electricity in Joya's village came and went without any pattern. Some days it stayed on all evening; other days it vanished at noon, returned for ten minutes, and vanished again. Nobody could plan anything. The supply was erratic: irregular and unpredictable. Behaviour can be erratic too, like a driver swerving between lanes for no reason. Erratic shares a root with error and errant, meaning to wander. Synonyms: inconsistent, unpredictable, capricious. Opposite: steady.

gre.s: The athlete's performances have been so ____ this season, brilliant one week and dismal the next, that even her coaches cannot predict how she will do.
gre.clue: brilliant one week and dismal the next

example: The old office printer was maddeningly erratic, working perfectly for an hour and then jamming on every second page.

en: Thorough and complete, covering every aspect
hook: EXHAUSTIVE: covers so much it EXHAUSTS the topic.
story: Exhaustive. Before buying a second-hand car, Mitu's father spent an entire Saturday inspecting it. He checked the engine, the brakes, every tyre, the paperwork, the service history, the rust under the doors, and even the radio. He test-drove it on three different kinds of road. When he finished, there was nothing left to check. His inspection was exhaustive: complete and thorough, covering every aspect. An exhaustive list includes every possible item.

gre.s: The committee's ____ report, which examined every expenditure over a ten-year period, left no question about where the funds had gone.
gre.clue: examined every expenditure over a ten-year period

example: Before writing her thesis on Bengali folk songs, Tahmina compiled an exhaustive list of every recording held in the national archive.

en: Possible to see coming or to predict in advance
hook: FORE-SEE-able: can be SEEN BEFORE it happens.
story: Foreseeable. Developers built a row of houses right on the riverbank, with no embankment and no drainage. Engineers warned them. Villagers warned them. The very first monsoon, the river swallowed three houses. Everyone said the disaster had been foreseeable: able to be predicted or expected. For the foreseeable future means as far ahead as we can reasonably predict. Fore means before, see means see.

gre.s: The collapse was entirely ____, since engineers had warned for years that the dam could not withstand a major flood.
gre.clue: engineers had warned for years

example: Given how little the twins had studied, their poor marks in the board exams were perfectly foreseeable.

en: Producing good or helpful results; productive
hook: FRUITFUL: a tree full of FRUIT.
story: Fruitful. Farhan expected the two-hour project meeting to be a waste of time, as usual. Instead, the team solved three long-standing problems, agreed on a budget, assigned every task, and planned the product launch. Everyone left energised. The meeting had been fruitful: producing good, helpful results. Picture a tree heavy with fruit. A fruitful discussion leads somewhere; a fruitless one wastes everyone's time.

gre.s: After decades of ____ research that yielded dozens of important discoveries, the laboratory was closed for lack of funding.
gre.clue: that yielded dozens of important discoveries

example: The partnership between the two chemists proved fruitful, producing a dozen papers and two patents within three years.

en: Of minor importance, occurring only alongside something bigger
hook: INCIDENTAL: just a side INCIDENT.
story: Incidental. Ishita joined the photography club only to learn how to use her new camera. But on the club's trips she made five close friends and discovered a love of travel. Those friendships were incidental benefits: they came along as minor side effects of her main purpose. Incidental means happening as a minor part or consequence of something more important. Incidental expenses are small extra costs, like rickshaw fares on a business trip. Contrast with essential or central.

gre.s: The lawyer argued that the photograph was merely ____ to the case, a minor detail that had no bearing on the central question of who signed the contract.
gre.clue: a minor detail that had no bearing on the central question

example: For the mountaineers, the stunning photographs were incidental, since their real goal was to measure how fast the glacier was shrinking.

en: So necessary that you cannot manage without it
hook: IN-DISPENSABLE: can NOT be dispensed with.
story: Indispensable. Arif's laptop is the centre of his life. His GRE practice tests, his freelance design work, his online banking, his video calls with his parents abroad, and every photo from the last five years all live inside it. When it broke for two days, his entire life stopped. It is indispensable: absolutely necessary, impossible to do without. In means not, dispensable means able to be dispensed with. A good teammate is indispensable.

gre.s: Once considered a luxury, reliable internet access has become ____ for students, who now need it to submit almost every assignment.
gre.clue: who now need it to submit almost every assignment

example: On long treks through the Bandarban hills, sturdy boots and plenty of drinking water are indispensable.

en: To restrain, hinder, or prevent
hook: INHIBIT: keeps you IN, holding you back.
story: Inhibit. Tanvir knew every answer in English class, but fear of making mistakes inhibited him from speaking. Every time he opened his mouth, his throat closed. His teacher started a small conversation club, and slowly he found his voice. To inhibit is to restrain, hinder, or prevent. Certain medicines inhibit the growth of bacteria. Inhibitions are feelings that hold you back socially. Think: keeps you in.

gre.s: Researchers hope the new compound will ____ the growth of tumors without damaging healthy tissue.
gre.clue: without damaging healthy tissue

example: Cold temperatures inhibit the growth of bacteria, which is why leftover rice should go into the fridge quickly.

en: Not giving the care or attention that duty requires
hook: NEGLIGENT: someone who NEGLECTS their duty.
story: Negligent. The night guard at the garment factory had one job: check the fire alarms and keep the gate secure. Instead, he slept every night on a plastic chair, the gate wide open, the alarm batteries long dead. When a small fire broke out, nobody heard a thing until the smoke reached the street. The inquiry called him negligent: failing to take the care that your duty requires. Negligent people neglect their responsibilities.

gre.s: The court ruled that the landlord had been ____, since he had ignored repeated warnings about the building's faulty wiring.
gre.clue: ignored repeated warnings

example: The hospital was found negligent after a nurse gave a patient the wrong medicine despite clear labels on every bottle.

en: Completely unaware of something, often what is close by
hook: OBLIVIOUS: in OBLIVION, totally unaware.
story: Oblivious. Mahin was so absorbed in his vocabulary app at Kamalapur station that he did not hear the announcements, did not notice the crowd boarding, and did not see his train pull away. When he finally looked up, the platform was empty. He had been oblivious: not aware of what was happening around him. Oblivious is usually followed by to or of. A related word is oblivion, the state of being forgotten. Synonyms: unaware, heedless, unmindful.

gre.s: Engrossed in her phone, the pedestrian remained completely ____ to the truck bearing down on her until a stranger grabbed her arm and pulled her back.
gre.clue: until a stranger grabbed her arm and pulled her back

example: Lost in a chess problem, Professor Haque was oblivious to the rain blowing through the open window onto his notes.

en: Done openly, where anyone can see it
hook: OVERT: right OVER the surface, out in the open.
story: Overt. In the past, governments spied secretly. Today, in some cities, surveillance is overt: cameras sit openly on every pole, clearly marked, so everyone knows they are being watched. At the office, the manager's dislike of Farhan was equally overt; he did not even try to hide it, rolling his eyes whenever Farhan spoke. Overt means done or shown openly, not secret. It is the opposite of covert. Think: right over the surface.

gre.s: Though the two nations avoided ____ hostilities, never firing a shot, they waged a fierce secret war through spies and proxies.
gre.clue: they waged a fierce secret war through spies and proxies

example: The referee somehow ignored an overt shove in the penalty area, and the whole stadium erupted in boos.

en: Showing deep, sharp insight; piercing
hook: PENETRATING: goes straight through to the truth.
story: Penetrating. In a job interview, Tanvir gave a polished answer about his strengths. The interviewer, an old engineer, looked at him for a long moment and asked one quiet question. "And what did you learn from the project that failed?" It cut straight through his rehearsed script. It was a penetrating question: sharp, insightful, piercing to the heart of the matter. A penetrating gaze seems to see right through you. Synonyms: incisive, perceptive, acute.

gre.s: Unlike most reviews, which merely summarized the plot, her ____ critique exposed the novel's hidden assumptions about class, insights that even the author later acknowledged.
gre.clue: Unlike most reviews, which merely summarized the plot

example: Her penetrating questions during the seminar forced the visiting economist to admit the weak points in his model.

en: Steady effort that keeps going in spite of setbacks
hook: PER-SEVERE-ANCE: persisting through SEVERE difficulty.
story: Perseverance. Hasan failed the civil service exam on his first attempt. He studied for another year and failed again, by only a few marks. His friends gave up and took other jobs. Hasan sat for it a third time, and this time he passed. Today he is an officer in Rangpur. He succeeded through perseverance: continued effort despite difficulty or delay. The verb is persevere. Think: per means through, so you push through severe times. Synonyms: persistence, tenacity, doggedness.

gre.s: The team's eventual success owed less to brilliance than to sheer ____: they repeated the failed experiment hundreds of times before obtaining a usable result.
gre.clue: they repeated the failed experiment hundreds of times

example: Learning the sitar demands years of perseverance, since even simple melodies can take months to sound right.

en: Not genuine; fake; a person who pretends
hook: PHONY: like a fake PHONE call from a 'bank'.
story: Phony. A man in a crisp white coat set up a stall at the Gabtoli bus terminal, selling a bottle of oil he promised would cure diabetes, baldness, and heartbreak. He called himself a doctor and displayed framed certificates. A curious student searched his name online: no such doctor existed. The certificates were phony: fake, not genuine. As a noun, a phony is a person who pretends. In The Catcher in the Rye, Holden calls almost everyone a phony. Synonyms: fake, sham, fraudulent.

gre.s: Investigators discovered that the charity was ____: the orphanage featured in its glossy brochures did not exist, and the donations had gone straight into the founder's bank account.
gre.clue: the orphanage featured in its glossy brochures did not exist

example: The phony job agency in Motijheel collected registration fees from hundreds of graduates and then vanished overnight.

en: Devoutly religious; sometimes, falsely or showily virtuous
hook: PIOUS: PRAYING faithfully.
story: Pious. Rahima Begum prays five times a day, fasts every Ramadan, and quietly sends money to an orphanage without telling anyone. Her neighbours consider her truly pious: devoutly religious. But pious has a second, sharper sense. When a corrupt businessman donates to a mosque only in front of cameras, people call it a pious show: falsely or showily virtuous. Synonyms for the first sense: devout, godly, reverent. For the second: sanctimonious, holier-than-thou. Opposite: irreverent.

gre.s: Voters grew weary of the senator's ____ sermons about honesty, especially once it emerged that he had lied repeatedly about his own finances.
gre.clue: once it emerged that he had lied repeatedly about his own finances

example: Her pious uncle spent the holy month in prayer and quiet study, refusing every invitation to travel or celebrate.

en: In its original, perfect condition; completely clean
hook: PRISTINE: PRIS-TEEN, as fresh and new as a teen.
story: Pristine. When Sara first visited Saint Martin's Island as a child, the beaches were pristine: white sand, clear turquoise water, coral glowing beneath the waves, and not a single plastic bottle in sight. Last year she returned. Wrappers drifted in the shallows and hotels crowded the shore. Pristine means in perfect, original condition, untouched and completely clean. A pristine copy of an old book has no marks at all.

gre.s: Conservationists are fighting to protect one of the last ____ forests on the continent, a wilderness never touched by logging or roads.
gre.clue: never touched by logging or roads

example: The museum's copy of the first edition is still pristine, its pages crisp and white after more than two centuries.

en: Outstanding skill, especially in a particular activity
hook: PROWESS: a PRO's skill.
story: Prowess. When Babu first joined the village football team, nobody noticed him. Then, in the final against the neighbouring union, he dribbled past four defenders and scored from thirty metres. The crowd carried him on their shoulders, and everyone talked about his prowess: exceptional skill or ability. Prowess comes from an old French word for valiant, and first meant bravery in battle. Now it means any outstanding skill: athletic, academic, or technical. Synonyms: expertise, mastery, virtuosity. Opposite: ineptitude.

gre.s: Despite her undoubted ____ as a chess player, she lost the championship because she could not cope with the pressure of the final game.
gre.clue: Despite her undoubted

example: The mechanic's prowess with old engines kept the village rice mill running long after spare parts had disappeared from the market.

en: To enjoy greatly; great enjoyment
bn: উপভোগ করা; তৃপ্তি সহকারে গ্রহণ করা
hook: RELISH: like a delicious RELISH sauce you savor.
story: Relish. After a year studying in Germany eating bread and pasta, Rafi came home to Dhaka. His mother placed a plate of shorshe ilish, hilsa fish in mustard sauce, in front of him. He ate slowly, closing his eyes with every bite, savouring every flavour. He relished it: enjoyed it greatly. You can also relish a challenge, relish a victory, or relish the chance to prove someone wrong. Think of a delicious relish sauce.

gre.s: Far from dreading the debate, the candidate seemed to ____ the chance to confront her opponent in front of a national audience.
gre.clue: Far from dreading the debate

example: The retired judge relished long afternoons in the university library, reading the history books he never had time for while working.

en: Making false spoken statements that damage someone's reputation
hook: SLANDER is SPOKEN; LIBEL is written.
story: Slander. After losing the student union election, Sabbir began telling everyone in the canteen that the winner had bought votes and cheated in exams. None of it was true, but the winner's reputation suffered. Sabbir was guilty of slander: making false spoken statements that damage someone's reputation. As a verb, to slander is to make such statements. Remember the difference: slander is spoken, while libel is written or published. Synonyms: defamation, calumny, smear. Opposite: praise.

gre.s: Unable to defeat his opponent on the issues, the candidate chose to ____ her instead, spreading false rumors that she had embezzled campaign funds.
gre.clue: spreading false rumors that she had embezzled campaign funds

example: Accusing a colleague of theft in front of the whole department, with no evidence at all, could expose you to a charge of slander.

en: Keeping careful watch for possible danger
hook: VIGILANT: keeping a VIGIL all night, watching.
story: Vigilant. During the dengue season, Sara's mother became a guard. Every evening she checked the flower pots, emptied any standing water, closed the windows at dusk, and inspected the children's arms for mosquito bites. She was vigilant: keeping careful watch for possible danger. A vigil is a night of staying awake to watch or pray, and vigilant people stay alert in the same way. Synonyms: watchful, alert, wary. Its opposite is careless or complacent.

gre.s: Security guards were told to remain ____ throughout the night, since thieves had already struck the warehouse twice in the small hours.
gre.clue: since thieves had already struck the warehouse twice

example: Parents in flood-prone villages stay vigilant throughout the monsoon, keeping small children well away from the swollen river.
